con.ukraine.t: Russia’s full-scale invasion of February 2022 continues along a front in the east and south, with independent assessments cited by Al Jazeera on 13 November 2026 putting Russia’s net gain this year at 117 sq km. Ukraine, Russia and the United States held their first talks since February in Abu Dhabi on 10–11 November; Russia’s delegation said it would be satisfied only by a peace on its terms, and an exchange of at least 1,000 prisoners a side was agreed. Ukraine says Russia fired 3,519 drones in ten days and 36 ballistic missiles at energy sites on 7 November.
con.gaza.t: A ceasefire signed by Israel and Hamas in October 2025 holds in name while Israel keeps the part of Gaza behind the ‘Yellow Line’. On 18 November 2026 Israeli tanks pushed into central Gaza east of Nuseirat and north of Bureij in the first broad ground operation since the truce; hospital officials said three Palestinians were killed, Hamas called it a flagrant violation, and Gaza’s health ministry counted seven dead in the previous 24 hours.
con.iran.n: Iran against the United States and Israel
con.iran.t: The United States and Israel opened a war on Iran on 28 February 2026 with about 900 strikes in under twelve hours; Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei was killed in the opening strikes and Mojtaba Khamenei was named his successor on 9 March. Pakistan brokered a two-week truce on 8 April, the US blockaded Iranian ports, and a preliminary agreement to end the war was announced on 14 June after 108 days. On 12 November 2026 Iran’s chief negotiator Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf called the position ‘no war and no peace’: the blockade and Iranian control of passage through the Strait of Hormuz remain, with Qatar mediating.
con.lebanon.t: Hezbollah fired rockets at Israel on 2 March 2026 after the killing of Iran’s supreme leader, and Israel answered with air raids and a ground invasion that left it holding a strip about 10 km deep. A US-brokered framework agreement signed in Washington on 26 June 2026 ties Israeli withdrawal to Hezbollah’s verified disarmament; by 29 July only one pilot zone, Zawtar al-Gharbiyeh, had passed to the Lebanese army, Israeli strikes continue, and Hezbollah rejects the deal.
con.yemen.parties: Houthis (Ansar Allah); Yemeni government and Southern forces; Saudi-led coalition
con.yemen.t: The Houthis, who took Sanaa in 2014, resumed a ground offensive in August 2026, besieged Taiz from early October and on 15 November drove government-aligned forces from the Bab al-Mandeb area; by 16 November they were reported 60–100 km from Aden, the government’s interim capital. The Saudi-led coalition has resumed air strikes and reports intercepting Houthi drones over Riyadh and Mecca; Saudi Arabia named a new Joint Forces commander on 16 November.
con.syria.parties: Syrian transitional government; Druze Sweida National Guard; Israel; remnants of ISIL
con.syria.t: Ahmad al-Shara’s government has run Damascus since Assad fell in December 2024, and a campaign in January 2026 brought the Kurdish-led SDF under its control after the US ended support. Sweida is the open front: an Israeli-backed Druze ‘National Guard’ holds the hills around the city, and The National reported on 22 October 2026 that Damascus had sent about 3,000 troops to its western approaches while Israel airlifts equipment into the province and keeps positions in Quneitra and Deraa.
con.sudan.parties: Sudanese Armed Forces; Rapid Support Forces and allies
con.sudan.t: The war between the Sudanese Armed Forces and the Rapid Support Forces began in April 2023; the RSF took El Fasher in October 2025 after a long siege and holds all five Darfur states. The army has turned the Kordofan front: on 13 November 2026 it took al-Khuwai in West Kordofan, having broken the siege of El Obeid, while the RSF still holds al-Nuhud and parts of South Kordofan with the SPLM-N.
con.myanmar.parties: Military government; People’s Defence Forces and ethnic armed organisations
con.myanmar.t: The civil war that followed the 2021 coup is in its sixth year. The military held phased elections in December 2025 and January 2026, coup leader Min Aung Hlaing was voted in as president, and on 6 November 2026 the election commission announced by-elections for 4 April 2027 in 39 constituencies, a third of them in areas of Sagaing, Mandalay and Chin where voting had been cancelled for security reasons.
con.drc.n: Eastern Congo: M23 and the FRN
con.drc.parties: DR Congo and allied Wazalendo militias; AFC/M23, renamed FRN, backed by Rwanda
con.drc.t: M23 took Goma and Bukavu in early 2025. A Doha framework of November 2025 and a roadmap agreed in Switzerland in August 2026 have not stopped the fighting: the rebel front, which Critical Threats reports was renamed FRN under Joseph Kabila on 12 October 2026, launched an offensive from Kahuzi-Biega on 6 November and took Bulambika and Bunyakiri on the RN3 by 9 November as government forces fell back toward Irangi.
con.somalia.parties: Somali government and AUSSOM; al-Shabaab; ISIL in Puntland
con.somalia.t: Al-Shabaab claimed on 26 October 2026 to have killed hundreds of Somali soldiers in an ambush near Leego, a toll not independently verified. Uganda, with about 6,500 troops in the country, said on 2 November it will withdraw by the end of 2027, and US forces left Baledogle airfield in late October while continuing air strikes, the latest on 5 November in Lower Shabelle (FDD’s Long War Journal, 10 November).
con.ethiopia.parties: Ethiopian federal forces and the Tigray Peace Force; TPLF; Fano; Eritrea
con.ethiopia.t: War returned to Tigray in late September 2026: federal forces took Mekelle in early October as the TPLF withdrew, Ethiopia and Eritrea severed ties on 2 October, and Addis Ababa accuses Eritrea of leading a rebel offensive, which Asmara denies. By 15 November Eritrean forces had reportedly retaken Badme, Fano fighters clashed with the army southeast of Bahir Dar on 16 November, and a UN delegation began a visit to Mekelle on 17 November (Critical Threats).
con.mali.n: Mali: JNIM and the Azawad front
con.mali.parties: Malian junta and Russia’s Africa Corps; JNIM; Azawad Liberation Front (FLA)
con.mali.t: JNIM’s fuel blockade of Bamako began on 3 September 2025. On 25 April 2026 JNIM and the Tuareg FLA attacked military sites across Mali including the capital, killed Defence Minister Sadio Camara at Kati and took Kidal with about 130 soldiers captured; Russia said its Africa Corps helped thwart a coup, and Assimi Goïta took the defence portfolio himself on 4 May. JNIM declared a full blockade of Bamako on 28 April.
con.burkina.parties: Burkinabè junta and VDP militias; JNIM; Islamic State Sahel
con.burkina.t: JNIM has fought in Burkina Faso since 2016 and in February 2026 made the country the focus of a coordinated offensive across the central Sahel and into Benin. Human Rights Watch documented the execution of at least 34 civilians at Titao on 14 February and four at Manni on 22 February, and ACLED counted more than 30 JNIM attacks that month with over 120 soldiers, forest guards and militiamen killed. The junta of Ibrahim Traoré has ruled since 2022.
con.niger.parties: Nigerien junta with Russian troops; Islamic State Sahel; JNIM
con.niger.t: Niger’s junta, in power since the 2023 coup, fights Islamic State’s Sahel affiliate in the west and JNIM in the south-east. Attackers struck the air base at Niamey’s Diori Hamani airport after midnight on 29 January 2026; ISIL claimed it, the government said 20 attackers were killed, and General Tiani thanked the Russian troops at the base and accused France, Benin and Ivory Coast of sponsoring the raid, without evidence. Attacks in Tillabéri in September 2025 killed more than 120 people.
con.haiti.parties: Haitian police and army with the Gang Suppression Force; Viv Ansanm and other gangs
con.haiti.t: The UN says up to 90% of Port-au-Prince is under gang control. The UN-backed Gang Suppression Force began arriving in April 2026 with a mandate to March 2027, and El Salvador sent up to 2,000 troops after four of its technicians were kidnapped on 18 October. On 19 November 2026 Haiti’s army and police, with a task force including Erik Prince’s Vectus Global, fought to clear Martissant on Route 2; police said 34 suspected gang members were killed.
con.mexico.parties: Mexican state; Sinaloa cartel factions; Jalisco New Generation Cartel (CJNG)
con.mexico.t: Mexican special forces killed CJNG leader Nemesio Oseguera Cervantes, ‘El Mencho’, at Tapalpa, Jalisco, on 22 February 2026 with US intelligence support; violence followed in at least 20 states. The Sinaloa cartel’s factions, orphaned by the detention of ‘El Chapo’ and ‘El Mayo’ in the US, fight an internal war that has killed thousands; on 11 November 2026 Mexico announced 15 arrests, 14 of them in Chiapas.
con.afpak.parties: Pakistan; Afghanistan’s Taliban government; Tehrik-i-Taliban Pakistan
con.afpak.t: Pakistan and the Afghan Taliban fought openly from late February 2026 after Pakistani air raids and an Afghan cross-border attack; a March ceasefire collapsed and Kabul struck targets in Balochistan and Khyber Pakhtunkhwa on 18 June. The UN counted at least 372 Afghan civilians killed in the first three months of 2026. Clashes continued at Angoor Adda and Torkham on 1 November, and on 11 November the TTP ambushed police in Kohat, killing ten (FDD’s Long War Journal, 12 November).
con.kashmir.parties: India; Pakistan; militant groups in Kashmir
con.kashmir.t: India struck nine sites in Pakistan on 6 May 2025 (‘Operation Sindoor’) after the Pahalgam attack of 22 April that killed 26, and a US-brokered ceasefire has held since May 2025. CFR’s tracker, updated 6 November 2026, records an Indian destroyer colliding with a Pakistani patrol vessel in the Arabian Sea on 15 September 2026, the first direct military confrontation since, and Indian border guards shooting Pakistani civilians in the Bedian sector on 2 October.
con.taiwan.parties: People’s Republic of China; Taiwan; United States
con.taiwan.t: China, which claims Taiwan and has not renounced force, massed more than 100 naval and coast guard vessels across the western Pacific in early November 2026 in unannounced drills larger than the ‘Justice Mission 2025’ exercise, with simulated attacks on cities and a submarine-launched intercontinental missile fired from the Yellow Sea. About 70 vessels were still inside the first island chain on 13 November as Beijing prepared to host APEC in Shenzhen; Taipei called it ‘silent intimidation’.
con.korea.parties: North Korea; South Korea; United States
con.korea.t: The 1953 armistice holds. North Korea fired several missiles from Sondok toward the East Sea on 4 November 2026 and said it had tested a new air-defence missile; in September it tested a hypersonic short-range system and commissioned a second Choe Hyon-class destroyer that Kim Jong Un called nuclear-capable. No US–North Korean talks are announced: Pyongyang wants Washington to drop denuclearisation first, while President Lee Jae Myung of South Korea urges sanctions relief for a freeze (Arms Control Today, October 2026).
con.karabakh.t: Azerbaijan took Nagorno-Karabakh in September 2023 and its Armenian population left. Pashinyan, Aliyev and Trump signed a declaration in Washington in August 2025; on 18 November 2026 Pashinyan said the 42 km TRIPP corridor across Armenia to Nakhchivan, with road, rail and pipelines, is ‘entering the practical implementation phase’ and that the southern border must now be delimited (Interfax). No peace treaty has been signed.
con.libya.parties: Government of National Unity (Dbeibah) and Tripoli militias; Libyan National Army (Haftar) and the eastern parliament
con.libya.t: Libya has had rival governments since 2014, Dbeibah’s in Tripoli and Haftar’s LNA in the east; the 2020 ceasefire froze the front at Sirte, and militia fighting flares in the capital. A UN-mediated ‘4+4’ roadmap signed in Tripoli on 30 August 2026 promises presidential and parliamentary elections within 24 months under a single executive, and the rival militaries have held unification talks and joint drills at Sirte under US supervision.
con.colombia.parties: Colombian state; ELN; FARC dissidents; Clan del Golfo (EGC); ACSN
con.colombia.t: Armed groups operate in 24 of Colombia’s 32 departments. Abelardo de la Espriella took office in August 2026 on a hard-line platform; Colombia Reports wrote on 11 November that in his first 90 days the Ombudsman and police recorded rises in homicide, extortion and attacks on the security forces, with 38 police and soldiers killed, and on 10 November the ELN hit a military base in Norte de Santander with a drone.
con.mozambique.parties: Mozambique with Rwandan forces; Islamic State Mozambique (al-Shabaab)
con.mozambique.t: The Islamic State-linked insurgency in Cabo Delgado began in 2017. IOM counted 1,235 people fleeing attacks or fear of attacks in Mocímboa da Praia, Macomia, Muidumbe and Meluco between 14 and 27 October 2026, 584 of them children. TotalEnergies restarted the Mozambique LNG project on 29 January 2026 after lifting force majeure, with first gas targeted for 2029.
con.nigeria.parties: Nigerian state; Boko Haram; ISWAP; Ansaru and bandit groups
con.nigeria.t: Boko Haram and ISWAP fight in the north-east, bandits and Ansaru in the north-west and centre, and the US struck targets it linked to Islamic State at Jabo in Sokoto on 25 December 2025 on the basis of Nigerian intelligence. The military said 48 fighters and one soldier died in a five-hour battle at Buni Yadi, Yobe, on 29–30 October 2026, and claimed 60 militants killed and 42 hostages freed in the week to 9 November; none of its figures is independently verified.
con.cameroon.parties: Cameroon; Ambazonian separatist groups; Boko Haram in the Far North
con.cameroon.t: Anglophone separatists have fought the state since 2017 in the North-West and South-West regions, while Boko Haram raids the Far North. The 2026 record runs from 15 civilians killed at Mbandfung on 14 January, through a separatist ceasefire for Pope Leo XIV’s visit to Bamenda on 15–17 April and school lockdowns in September, to four civilians killed at Koshin, Menchum, on 28 October (Wikipedia timeline, citing Xinhua and CrisisWatch).
con.philippines.parties: Philippine armed forces; New People’s Army; ISIL-linked groups in Mindanao
con.philippines.t: The communist New People’s Army insurgency dates from 1969. The army’s 4th Infantry Division said on 29 July 2026 that it had dismantled the North Eastern Mindanao Regional Committee and declared Caraga stable, reporting 11 encounters and 20 guerrillas ‘neutralised’ from April to June, and moved operations to Northern Mindanao.
con.iraq.t: US forces left their last Iraqi bases as the anti-ISIL coalition mandate expired on 30 September 2026, ending a 12-year mission; a UN report puts ISIL at ‘its weakest’ with a few hundred fighters, though Iraqi officers told Reuters its cells planned attacks to mark the withdrawal. Baghdad’s deadline for militias to surrender weapons has slipped to June 2027, and the Kurdistan region counted more than 1,000 drone and missile attacks since the Iran war began on 28 February.
con.venezuela.parties: United States; Venezuelan interim government; armed colectivos and cross-border groups
con.venezuela.t: US forces seized Nicolás Maduro and his wife in Caracas on 3 January 2026 and flew them to New York, where he faces narco-terrorism charges; Delcy Rodríguez was sworn in as president on 5 January. On 2 November Secretary Rubio set out a three-phase plan of stabilisation, recovery and democratic transition, and on 18 November Pete Hegseth visited Caracas and signed an agreement restoring military ties; no election date is set, and AP counts at least 240 killed in US strikes on alleged drug boats since September 2025.
con.southsudan.parties: South Sudan government forces; SPLA-IO (Machar); ethnic militias
con.southsudan.t: The 2018 peace deal is close to collapse: Riek Machar is detained, and fighting between government forces and his SPLA-IO spread to Ruweng from 4 October 2026, killing at least 23 and, by the information minister’s count, displacing more than 100,000 (AFP, 8 November). National elections, the first since independence in 2011, are set for 22 December 2026 after several postponements.
con.car.parties: CAR government with Russia’s Africa Corps; FPRC, MDRPC and other armed groups
con.car.t: President Touadéra’s government relies on Russia’s Africa Corps, Wagner’s successor, whose transition is described as incomplete. Armed groups including elements of the FPRC and the MDRPC attacked the Am-Dafok border post in Vakaga, on the Sudanese frontier, on 30 June 2026, according to MINUSCA (African Arguments, 3 August 2026).
con.ecuador.parties: Ecuadorian state; Los Choneros, Los Lobos and allied gangs tied to Mexican and Albanian networks
con.ecuador.t: Ecuador recorded 9,216 intentional homicides in 2025, about 51 per 100,000, the most on record; January to August 2026 ran 6.4% lower. Daniel Noboa decreed a state of exception on 15 September 2026 and a night curfew in Guayas, Manabí, Los Ríos and El Oro to 30 September, which produced 2,561 detentions; El Universo reported US troops joining some operations (The Rio Times, 5 October).
con.pkk.t: The PKK announced its dissolution and disarmament in 2025 at Abdullah Öcalan’s call, held a symbolic weapons-burning in northern Iraq and withdrew fighters from Turkey, but co-founder Murat Karayilan said on 30 April 2026 that the process was ‘frozen’ after Ankara missed an April deadline for peace legislation; President Erdoğan says it ‘is proceeding as it should’ (AP).
con.balochistan.parties: Pakistan; Baloch Liberation Army and allied groups
con.balochistan.t: Baloch separatists fight the Pakistani state and Chinese-linked projects in the south-west. The Baloch Liberation Army said on 16 November 2026 that its drone unit had killed six security personnel in four strikes between 5 and 14 November at camps in Mastung and Kalat; Pakistan’s ISPR confirmed two deaths from one drone attack, and none of the other claims is independently verified (IANS, 17 November).
con.naxal.t: Chhattisgarh’s deputy chief minister Vijay Sharma said on 31 March 2026, the day the Centre’s deadline to end Left-Wing Extremism expired, that armed Naxal cadres in the state had been ‘completely eliminated’, citing more than 3,000 surrenders, 2,000 arrests and over 500 killed in two years; about 400 interior police camps in Bastar are to be converted to civil use and most paramilitary forces may leave by March 2027 (PTI). The claims are the government’s own.
con.papua.parties: Indonesia; West Papua National Liberation Army (TPNPB-OPM)
con.papua.t: The TPNPB, armed wing of the Free Papua Movement, fights Indonesian forces in the highlands. It shot dead eight gold miners at Yahukimo on 20 May 2026, calling them disguised soldiers, which the military denied, and on 9 September killed three agriculture officials near Wamena; the National Commission on Human Rights is investigating a military operation at Kembru in April in which more than a dozen civilians died (The Jakarta Post; The Star).
con.scs.parties: China; the Philippines; Vietnam, Malaysia and others
con.scs.t: China’s coast guard and maritime militia contest Philippine access to Scarborough Shoal and Second Thomas Shoal. On 23–24 July 2026 twelve Chinese coast guard and three militia vessels hit two Philippine ships with water cannon at Scarborough and came within 7 metres of a fisheries boat; on 20 July a Filipino sailor was struck with a baton at Second Thomas Shoal, both sides summoned ambassadors, and Marco Rubio reaffirmed the US defence treaty in Manila.
